subtitle: Restorative approaches tie accountability to what actually happened at work. You will learn to connect it to what needs to change and to how appropriate repair will be checked.
scope: For DHS leaders and supervisors. This optional course practices everyday accountability and work-related repair. It does not train facilitators, create a new complaint process, replace investigation or discipline, or require employees to participate in an informal conversation. Actual concerns follow current agency procedures, applicable policies and responsible HR guidance. Use practice details in learning responses; keep personnel information in approved channels.
introTranscript: Repairing workplace harm involves more than arranging an apology. Leaders need to understand the effect on the work, preserve appropriate routes for concerns, and connect responsibility to a practical change. A restorative approach asks what happened, who or what was affected, and what a responsible next step could address. It is not a promise that everyone will agree, forgive or resume a close relationship. You will practice explaining the choice to participate, preparing a useful conversation when appropriate, turning commitments into work changes and reviewing follow-through. Staff remain responsible for their own work, while the consultant can offer guidance and feedback. The cases are invented and do not determine the outcome of a real concern.

lessons.title: Begin with the effect and the responsibility
lessons.summary: Distinguish repairing a work effect from obtaining quick emotional closure.
lessons.objective: Describe a practice work effect without guessing either person’s motives.
objectives: Describe a practice work effect without guessing either person’s motives.
Connect an appropriate correction to the specific effect it addresses.
Distinguish an everyday repair practice from a formal workplace determination.
takeaways: An apology and a work correction serve different purposes.
Repair needs a clear link to the effect.
Appropriate formal handling remains in place.
lessons.statement: The practical question is what responsibility follows from the effect, not how quickly the room can look comfortable again.

image.caption: A useful repair question connects an interaction to its effect on the work.

intro.heading: Ask what needs to be made right
intro.body:
A leader notices that an employee’s contribution was dismissed during a meeting. The employee later says the exchange affected whether their evidence was considered. Arranging an apology may matter, but it does not automatically return that evidence to the decision. A practical repair begins by identifying the effect and the responsibility that can address it. It asks what happened in the work and what can appropriately change.

Minnesota’s Office of Collaboration and Dispute Resolution describes restorative practices as approaches that support relationships and repair harm. This course applies a limited everyday work lens: understand the effect, clarify responsibility and review a suitable correction. It does not confer facilitation credentials or make every concern suitable for a shared conversation. Leaders must still obtain responsible guidance and follow actual policy and procedures.

Separate three questions. What words, actions or arrangements can be described? What effect was observed or reported? What responsibility does the leader or another authorized role have now? The answers may not be complete, and different people may give different accounts. Keep the account specific without making uncertainty an excuse to ignore a clear practical problem. You can preserve a contribution in the work process while the appropriate office considers any formal concern.

Emotional closure is a different question. An employee may appreciate an apology, remain uncertain, prefer a limited working relationship or need time. The leader cannot prescribe forgiveness as evidence that the matter is over. Likewise, a person’s sincere regret does not establish that every effect has been addressed. Ask whether the relevant contribution, access, behavior or expectation has changed in a way that can be examined.

Use invented examples here. For an actual concern, records, facts and conclusions belong in the responsible agency channels. The purpose of learning is to improve a next decision: notice the effect, identify an appropriate correction and retain the process needed for a fair response.

inThisLesson: Describe what happened in the work.
lessons.keyStatement: Connect the correction to the effect rather than using a visible apology as the entire measure of repair.

flashcards.back: A consequence for contribution, participation, access or another work activity that can be described and examined.
Taking appropriate responsibility for an action and following through on a suitable correction.
An action intended to address a specific effect; its usefulness needs follow-through.
How a person feels about what happened; a leader cannot require a prescribed feeling as proof of success.
The actual agency process for a workplace concern, separate from this course’s optional practice.
A description that distinguishes observed information, reported experience and what remains uncertain.

items.title: An apology without a work correction
items.body: If the effect involved a contribution being excluded from a decision, ask how that contribution will be appropriately considered. The apology may be meaningful, but it answers a different question. A useful plan identifies the authorized review, the person responsible and the point at which the work effect will be checked.

items.title: A correction without listening
items.body: A leader may choose a convenient action that does not address the effect reported. Ask a neutral question about the work consequence without requiring the person to share personal history or educate the team. Listening informs the correction; it does not transfer responsibility for responding to the person affected.

items.title: An uncertain account
items.body: Avoid announcing a complete finding from a partial description. Preserve the appropriate process and ask what practical step is justified now. For example, reconsidering a contribution through its responsible review can address a work question without deciding every motive or complaint outcome. Keep each decision within its actual authority.

tabs.label: Action
tabs.body: Action describes what occurred in the interaction or arrangement. A remark that dismissed evidence gives a practical starting point; an identity label does not identify what must change. Keep motive and formal findings separate from the observed act. This helps the leader preserve appropriate accountability without turning an everyday repair question into an improvised personnel assessment.

tabs.label: Effect
tabs.body: Effect identifies the consequence being addressed and how it is known. A person may report exclusion while a work record shows their evidence was omitted. Those accounts can inform a correction without establishing every cause. Ask what needs an appropriate response, avoiding both dismissal of the experience and a promise that one action will resolve every effect.

tabs.label: Responsibility
tabs.body: Responsibility identifies the role that can make the correction and the role handling any formal matter. An apology may acknowledge conduct, while the authorized person decides how evidence is considered. A shared discussion cannot confer extra decision powers or remove duties. Naming these roles prevents repair from becoming a ceremonial promise with no work owner.

check.question: An employee’s evidence was dismissed in a meeting. The leader arranges an apology but leaves the evidence out of the decision. What is missing?
check.correct: An appropriate work correction that addresses whether the evidence should be considered, alongside the responsible process for the concern.
wrong: A requirement that the employee publicly forgive the speaker.
A claim that the apology proves every effect has ended.
A group vote on whether the employee’s experience deserves attention.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response connects repair to the reported work effect without demanding a particular emotional outcome.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Public forgiveness cannot determine whether omitted evidence received proper consideration. An apology does not prove every work effect ended. A group vote cannot decide whether a person’s experience deserves attention. Identify the correction to the actual effect and the responsible route while leaving emotional responses free of a prescribed outcome.

items.text: The relevant evidence was left out of the review.
The authorized person will reconsider the evidence on its merits.
The employee must say the apology resolved every concern.
A meeting arrangement prevented a colleague from contributing.
The chair will change the arrangement and check whether it becomes usable.
Everyone must describe feeling comfortable by the end of the meeting.

lessons.next: Next, examine whether a conversation is appropriate and genuinely chosen.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: During a service-notice review, Lena’s access evidence is dismissed through a personal remark. Leader Ellis arranges an apology, but the decision proceeds without the evidence. Lena does not want to make a public statement about forgiveness.
scenario.prompt: Which response best connects responsibility to the effect?
options: Require Lena to accept the apology before the evidence can be considered.
Declare the review complete because Ellis arranged an apology.
Use the responsible process for the concern and return the evidence to its appropriate review without requiring an emotional statement.
responses: This makes work participation conditional on a prescribed response.
The apology does not establish that the decision considered relevant evidence.
This addresses the work effect while preserving choice and formal responsibilities.

lessons.transfer: For an invented meeting, identify an action, a reported work effect and one appropriate correction. State separately what the correction cannot establish.

move.control: You can connect a practical correction to the effect and retain responsible handling.
move.failure: A visible apology becomes a substitute for reviewing the contribution or changing the arrangement.
move.next: When planning the next appropriate correction, ask which specific work effect it addresses and how that will be checked.

lessons.title: Make the choice to participate real
lessons.summary: Explain purpose, limits and alternatives without making informal dialogue the price of support.
lessons.objective: Write an invitation that explains a conversation’s purpose and limits.
objectives: Write an invitation that explains a conversation’s purpose and limits.
Identify a condition that makes participation coercive.
Preserve actual formal routes and leader duties when a person declines dialogue.
takeaways: An invitation must explain what participation involves.
Declining dialogue does not erase a concern.
Actual procedures govern available routes and duties.
lessons.statement: A person’s choice is not meaningful if support or work access depends on accepting the invitation.

image.caption: A clear invitation explains the purpose and the choices before a conversation begins.

intro.heading: Explain the invitation before seeking agreement
intro.body:
A leader may believe that bringing people together demonstrates fairness. But a shared conversation can be unhelpful or inappropriate when the purpose is unclear, the power difference is substantial, a safety question exists, or the invitation carries a hidden penalty. Begin with the responsible process for the actual concern. Do not invent a rule that every employee must confront another person before receiving support or using a formal route.

When an informal conversation is appropriate, explain what it is intended to address. “We could discuss how the review meeting affected participation and whether a practical change would help” is different from “You both must meet so this can be closed.” Describe who would be present, what the facilitator or leader can and cannot do, and how next steps would be decided. Check relevant information and records requirements rather than promising unlimited confidentiality.

Make the alternatives understandable. The State’s Respectful Workplace policy describes informal options and formal complaint routes within its scope. Other actual concerns may fall under different policies or procedures. Use current agency guidance to explain the appropriate choices and any duties the leader retains. This course is not an instruction to halt required action while waiting for agreement to talk.

Power matters to the invitation. A supervisor controls assignments, evaluations or schedules in ways a colleague may notice even when the supervisor does not intend pressure. Avoid tying project access, development opportunities or a favorable assessment to accepting the conversation. Ask whether the person can decline this particular invitation without losing the support or appropriate work arrangement they need.

Agreement to one conversation is not an agreement to every outcome. A participant may set an appropriate limit, ask for clarification or decide that the approach is not useful. Explain how those choices will be handled through responsible guidance. A well-prepared invitation makes the work question clear and preserves formal responsibilities, rather than treating consent as a one-time signature that gives the leader control over the person’s experience.

For covered managers and supervisors, MMB Policy 1436 requires immediate reporting of protected-class harassment or discrimination allegations or incidents to human resources or the agency Affirmative Action Officer, followed by current agency procedures. A learning exercise, check-in or optional repair conversation does not postpone that duty. Other matters follow their applicable policy and responsible route; do not conduct a course-based investigation.

lessons.keyStatement: Preserve the person’s meaningful choice while carrying out the responsibilities of the leader’s role.

accordion.heading: Check whether the choice is genuine

items.title: Participation tied to a project
items.body: If the employee must attend an informal conversation to stay on a project, the invitation carries a work consequence. Remove the invented condition and use responsible guidance for appropriate work arrangements. An optional discussion should not quietly become a new eligibility test for participation or development.

items.title: A promise of complete confidentiality
items.body: The leader may have duties that limit what can be kept private, and actual records have applicable rules. Explain the real limits before inviting disclosure, using responsible guidance. Do not promise that everything will remain off the record or use a course response as a place to store personnel information.

items.title: A person declines the meeting
items.body: A declined invitation does not establish that the concern was unimportant or that the employee refuses all support. Ask which appropriate route or arrangement remains useful without demanding an explanation of private reasons. The leader still carries out actual policy responsibilities and follows current procedures.

tabs.label: Purpose
tabs.body: Purpose names the work question and realistic benefit. Reconsidering how evidence enters review is more concrete than requiring everyone to trust each other immediately. Explain what the conversation could address, without treating attendance as proof of goodwill. The person’s choice and the leader’s actual responsibilities should remain distinct throughout the invitation.

tabs.label: Limits
tabs.body: Limits explain participants, process and authority. Do not promise a formal finding, absolute secrecy or immediate emotional closure the leader cannot deliver. A clear limit makes consent more informed and preserves required routes. If the matter is unsuitable for this process, responsible guidance should shape the next step instead of forcing a shared meeting to appear successful.

tabs.label: Choices
tabs.body: Choices identify appropriate alternatives if the person does not choose the conversation. Declining an optional discussion does not automatically mean refusing repair or losing access to a formal process. The leader still carries required action and reporting. Explain the actual next route without making support contingent on attendance or creating a new complaint prerequisite.

check.question: A leader says an employee can use a formal complaint route only after attending a restorative meeting. What should the leader do?
check.correct: Remove the invented prerequisite and use current responsible guidance to explain the actual routes, options and leader duties.
wrong: Keep the prerequisite because a shared conversation always resolves harm.
Treat declining the meeting as proof that the employee does not want repair.
Offer confidentiality that the leader has not checked in order to secure attendance.
check.feedbackCorrect: The invitation does not create a new barrier to an actual agency process.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A shared conversation cannot universally resolve harm or create a complaint prerequisite. Declining the meeting does not establish that the person rejects repair. An unchecked confidentiality promise makes the invitation less informed. Remove the invented gate and explain actual options and leader duties through responsible guidance.

items.text: The purpose and possible next steps are explained before agreement.
Project participation depends on attending the meeting.
The leader has not checked the applicable information-handling limits.
The invitation explains appropriate alternatives without declaring the concern resolved.
Declining the invitation is described as a sign of poor commitment.
The leader is unsure which policy route applies to the actual concern.

lessons.next: Next, prepare a conversation suited to the work question and the people involved.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Supervisor Marta invites Devin and Chloe to discuss a difficult project exchange. She says Devin will regain the lead assignment only if both attend and agree the issue is closed. Devin asks about another route for the concern.
scenario.prompt: What change is needed before the invitation can be considered?
options: Remove the assignment condition and closure demand, clarify actual options with responsible guidance, and keep leader duties in place.
Repeat the invitation until Devin agrees because attendance proves commitment.
Tell Devin that a formal route would show unwillingness to collaborate.
responses: This separates optional dialogue from work pressure and preserves appropriate handling.
Repeated pressure does not make participation voluntary or useful.
Collaboration language should not become a barrier to a legitimate agency route.

lessons.transfer: Write a practice invitation with purpose, participants, checked limits and appropriate alternatives. Identify any work condition that would make the choice coercive.

move.control: You can explain the invitation accurately and avoid attaching invented penalties to the decision.
move.failure: A leader offers choice in words while making support or work access depend on attendance.
move.next: Review the next suitable invitation for hidden conditions before asking someone to agree.

lessons.title: Prepare for a useful conversation
lessons.summary: Choose a manageable work question, appropriate support and a process that does not amplify the harm.
lessons.objective: Define a specific work question that a conversation can address.
objectives: Define a specific work question that a conversation can address.
Identify preparation gaps involving power, access or role conflicts.
Explain why complex situations may require responsible trained support rather than a leader improvising.
takeaways: A manageable question is easier to address than a demand for total agreement.
Preparation includes access and role clarity.
Not every situation fits the same conversation.
lessons.statement: Preparation helps people understand the work before them and the responsibilities that remain outside the room.

image.caption: A prepared discussion keeps the purpose, roles and limits understandable.

intro.heading: Reduce uncertainty without predetermining the answer
intro.body:
A conversation can begin badly even when the leader intends care. One participant arrives expecting an opportunity to explain a work effect. Another expects the employee to withdraw a concern. The leader expects an apology and immediate closure. Preparation exposes these mismatched expectations before a shared meeting makes them harder to address. The aim is a clear, suitable purpose, not a script that forces the desired ending.

Start with a manageable work question. “How can the review process consider each relevant contribution?” gives people something concrete to examine. “How can we make everyone trust each other again?” may describe a hope, but it is not a result the leader can promise. Define what the conversation can affect and what remains with the responsible process or authorized decision-maker.

Check role conflicts. A supervisor who controls an employee’s assessment may not be perceived as a neutral facilitator. A person handling a formal concern has responsibilities that should not be blurred with an informal discussion. Obtain appropriate guidance about roles, support and suitability. This optional course develops leadership judgment; it does not qualify a leader to facilitate every conflict or serious workplace situation alone.

Plan for usable participation. Consider the meeting format, time to prepare, clear written information and ways to request relevant support through the appropriate channel. Do not assume a person’s preference from identity or require private details to justify a practical format question. A conversation about participation should not recreate the same access barrier that contributed to the problem.

Finally, plan what happens if the discussion cannot proceed usefully. A pause is not proof of failure by a participant. The leader can summarize the work question, stop an inappropriate exchange and return to responsible guidance. Preparation creates a route for continuation, limits and follow-through. It does not guarantee that everyone will agree, that all facts are settled or that the formal concern can be closed.

lessons.keyStatement: A clear purpose and honest role boundaries are more useful than a promise that one meeting will resolve everything.

items.title: The purpose is too broad
items.body: Turn a general hope into a work question people can examine. A leader cannot guarantee restored trust by the end of a meeting, but can ask how a contribution will be heard or a handoff clarified. State the limited result and preserve other responsibilities so the discussion does not become a demand for complete reconciliation.

items.title: The leader has several roles
items.body: A leader may supervise the work, receive a concern and wish to facilitate. Those roles are not interchangeable. Seek responsible guidance about what should remain separate and what support is appropriate. Do not claim neutrality merely because the leader intends fairness or knows both participants well.

items.title: The format creates a barrier
items.body: Offer a clear way to ask about usable participation before the meeting. Explain the question in advance and choose a suitable arrangement within actual authority. Use the relevant accommodation or support process where applicable; do not require sensitive details in group preparation notes or assume needs from identity.

tabs.label: Question
tabs.body: A question defines what the discussion can usefully change. “How will contributions enter review?” can guide a practical arrangement; “How will everyone forgive?” prescribes a personal outcome. State boundaries so participants can contribute without assuming the meeting decides a case. If the issue needs another authority, route it rather than broadening the promise.

tabs.label: Roles
tabs.body: Roles identify participants, facilitation support and responsible decision-makers. A supervisor who controls an evaluation also has power in the conversation; calling themselves neutral does not remove it. Examine suitability and potential conflicts with responsible guidance. Acknowledging the role difference is more useful than asking the employee to accept an unexplained arrangement.

tabs.label: Conditions
tabs.body: Conditions include usable information, participation arrangements and a pause route. A short meeting can still reproduce an access barrier or place someone under pressure. Prepare the format and next steps rather than assuming good intention makes them unnecessary. The plan supports an appropriate discussion; it does not guarantee agreement or qualify a leader for every conflict.

check.question: A supervisor promises to act as a neutral facilitator while also deciding an employee’s evaluation and handling the concern. What needs attention?
check.correct: The role conflict and the suitability of the process should be examined with responsible guidance before proceeding.
wrong: The supervisor’s good intention automatically removes the power difference.
A short meeting makes preparation unnecessary.
The employee should agree to all roles before receiving an explanation.
check.feedbackCorrect: Preparation recognizes the actual roles and seeks a process suited to the situation.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Good intention does not remove a supervisor’s evaluation power or handling responsibilities. A brief meeting can still need substantial preparation. Asking the employee to agree before roles are explained prevents informed choice. Examine the role conflict and suitability with responsible guidance and clarify the process before proceeding.

items.text: The invitation names one work question and what remains outside the discussion.
The leader guarantees trust will be restored by the end.
The facilitator also controls the participant’s evaluation.
A pause route and next responsible step are explained.
The meeting is described as a substitute for every formal procedure.
The proposed format repeats the participation barrier being discussed.

lessons.next: Next, practice listening and accountability without making either person perform a prescribed story.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Leader Omar plans a discussion after an unresolved handoff dispute. He supervises both participants and has received a formal concern about the same exchange. The invitation promises to restore trust in one session, and the agenda is not shared in advance.
options: Proceed because Omar knows both employees and therefore has no role conflict.
Obtain responsible guidance about role separation and suitability, define a limited work question, and explain usable participation and next steps.
Require both participants to promise trust before receiving the agenda.
responses: Familiarity does not erase formal responsibilities or supervisory power.
This makes the purpose, roles and conditions clearer without promising an outcome beyond the discussion.
Trust cannot be required as an entry condition for understanding the process.

lessons.transfer: Prepare an invented discussion plan with a specific question, roles, authority limits, participation conditions and a pause route. Identify one matter that requires responsible guidance.

move.control: You can clarify the work question and seek suitable support rather than improvising beyond your role.
move.failure: The leader enters a complex situation with an unclear purpose, conflicting roles and a promised ending.
move.next: Before the next appropriate discussion, write one sentence about what it can address and one about what remains elsewhere.

lessons.title: Listen for the effect and the next responsibility
lessons.summary: Use specific accounts and questions while avoiding forced agreement, disclosure or apologies.
lessons.objective: Use a neutral question to clarify a reported work effect.
objectives: Use a neutral question to clarify a reported work effect.
Distinguish acknowledging an account from declaring every fact settled.
Identify language that invites responsibility without forcing personal disclosure or an apology.
takeaways: Listening can clarify without deciding the entire concern.
Acknowledgment does not require identical accounts.
Accountability is more specific than a rehearsed apology.
lessons.statement: People can describe an effect and consider a next action without being required to tell the same story.

image.caption: Specific questions connect an account to the practical work that follows.

intro.heading: Ask questions that support understanding
intro.body:
During a conversation, a leader may try to remove discomfort by asking everyone to agree on one version of the event. That can make the discussion a contest over whose experience counts. A useful approach separates the supported account, the reported effect and the practical next responsibility. Agreement about every interpretation is not always needed to identify a work change that should be considered.

Begin with a neutral question. “What part of the handoff became difficult, and what information was missing?” invites a work account. “Why did you overreact?” begins with a judgment about the person. “Tell us about your culture so we understand you” may create an unwanted educational burden. Ask about the relevant interaction and effect without requiring personal history or a group identity explanation.

Listen for specifics and clarify the source of the account. A person may describe what they observed, what they were told and what they concluded. These are related but different. Summarize carefully: “You are saying the changed review order meant your evidence was not considered before the deadline.” The summary checks understanding. It does not announce that all formal facts or motives are settled.

Invite responsibility through behavior and work. “What could you do differently at the next review?” gives someone a concrete question. A demanded apology can produce words without a workable change. A suitable acknowledgment may still matter, but do not dictate the affected person’s acceptance, require mutual blame or assume the situation is equally shared. Actual findings and duties belong with the responsible process.

If the exchange becomes dismissive, unsafe or inconsistent with the agreed limits, use the appropriate pause and guidance. Returning to the question is useful only when it preserves a suitable process; it is not a reason to keep every conversation going. Listening is an active leadership practice: ask a clear question, check understanding, retain uncertainty honestly and connect any useful information to an appropriate responsibility.

inThisLesson: Ask about the relevant work effect.
Use a pause when the process becomes unsuitable.
lessons.keyStatement: Acknowledge what was reported, clarify what is known and ask what responsibility can address the work.

items.title: “What did this change for your work?”
items.body: This invites the person to explain a relevant effect without prescribing the emotional response or requiring personal history. Follow with a specific clarification if needed. The answer can inform a practical correction while formal facts remain with the responsible process. Do not turn the question into a public demand to prove worthiness.

items.title: “Can you both accept equal blame?”
items.body: A shared conversation does not establish equal responsibility. The question can pressure people into an artificial balance that makes the leader comfortable. Examine the actual behavior, effect and responsibilities instead. Do not use participation to require a person to withdraw a concern or accept an unsupported conclusion.

items.title: “What would you change next time?”
items.body: This invites an actionable response, such as preserving a contribution or checking a handoff. Ask how the change would work and who has authority for it. A vague statement about being nicer may need clarification. The response should address the effect rather than become a test of whether the affected person forgives.

tabs.label: Account
tabs.body: An account asks what was observed or reported without imposing a character or identity explanation. The relevant issue might be an omitted contribution rather than the whole personal relationship. Keep inquiry specific and information handling appropriate. A broad personal disclosure demand can add burden without clarifying the work effect the leader needs to address.

tabs.label: Understanding
tabs.body: Understanding checks whether the leader heard the account accurately. Summarizing a reported effect and inviting correction is different from announcing a formal finding. It can locate a useful responsibility while facts remain uncertain. Avoid forced equal blame: two people participating does not establish that each had identical responsibility for what occurred.

tabs.label: Responsibility
tabs.body: Responsibility asks what action could address the identified effect within authority. It does not require accepting an apology or prescribing forgiveness. The leader can clarify an appropriate correction and preserve formal handling without making the employee responsible for the response. A useful discussion links accountability to the work instead of securing a predetermined emotional statement.

check.question: A participant describes evidence being left out. Which leader response best checks understanding?
check.correct: “You are saying the review moved ahead without that evidence being considered. Have I understood the work effect accurately?”
wrong: “Explain your entire cultural background so the team can judge the reaction.”
“Can everyone agree you were both equally responsible?”
“Accept the apology now so we can prove repair is complete.”
check.feedbackCorrect: The response checks the reported effect without demanding personal disclosure or a predetermined judgment.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A complete cultural-background account is not needed to check whether evidence was considered. Forced equal blame supplies a judgment instead of understanding the effect. Requiring apology acceptance imposes closure. Summarize the reported work consequence neutrally, invite correction and keep formal findings and next responsibilities in their proper roles.

items.text: Ask whether the summary accurately describes the work effect.
Require both people to admit equal blame without examining their actions.
Identify a change to the next evidence handoff and who can make it.
Separate what was observed from what was inferred.
Make forgiveness the evidence that the leader’s response succeeded.
Ask how a contribution will be retained in the next review.

lessons.next: Next, turn an appropriate commitment into an action that can be checked.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: In an appropriate project discussion, Priya explains that her evidence was not considered after a dismissive exchange. Colleague Scott has a different account of the sequence. Leader June asks both to agree they were equally responsible before discussing the review process.
options: Treat disagreement as proof that no practical work change can be considered.
Ask Priya to accept Scott’s account as the price of continued participation.
Clarify the reported effect and supported sequence, avoid forced equal blame, and examine a specific work correction within the appropriate process.
responses: Different accounts do not automatically prevent a justified practical review.
This replaces clarification with pressure and makes participation conditional.
This preserves uncertainty honestly and connects the discussion to responsibility.

lessons.transfer: Write a neutral question, an understanding-check summary and an invitation to identify a specific next responsibility for an invented work exchange.

move.control: You can ask specific questions and check understanding without imposing one story or a prescribed emotion.
move.failure: The discussion becomes a demand for shared blame or a performance of agreement.
move.next: In the next suitable discussion, summarize the work effect and invite correction before asking about a next action.

lessons.title: Turn responsibility into a usable repair plan
lessons.summary: Define an action, owner, work boundary and check without promising authority that the group does not hold.
lessons.objective: Write a repair action connected to a specific work effect.
objectives: Write a repair action connected to a specific work effect.
Identify the authority and responsibility needed to carry out the action.
Choose a follow-through check that examines change without requiring forgiveness.
takeaways: A practical commitment says who will do what.
The action must fit actual authority.
A check examines the effect, not the required feeling.
lessons.statement: A repair plan becomes useful when a person can recognize the action, its owner and the evidence that will be reviewed.

image.caption: A clear action plan keeps responsibility visible after the conversation.

intro.heading: Make the commitment concrete
intro.body:
A discussion ends with agreement to “communicate better.” The phrase may express goodwill, but it leaves the next review unchanged. No one knows who will send the evidence, how it will be considered or what happens if the problem returns. A usable repair plan connects a specific action to the work effect and names the responsibility needed to carry it out.

Begin with the effect the action addresses. If a relevant contribution was omitted, an appropriate action might be to return it to the authorized review and clarify the evidence handoff. If an arrangement blocked participation, the action might involve a suitable change to that arrangement. The plan should not guarantee that every recommendation will be accepted. Fair consideration and a particular decision outcome are different results.

Name the owner and actual authority. The meeting chair may change an agenda practice, while a decision-maker retains authority over a policy or service choice. A leader cannot promise a promotion, change employment terms or close a formal concern simply because participants discussed an issue. Use responsible guidance for matters beyond the conversation’s scope, and explain the limit in plain language.

Choose a check that examines the action and effect. Was the agreed information provided? Was the contribution considered through the relevant process? Did the changed arrangement become usable? What remains uncertain? The affected person may choose to provide useful feedback, but the plan should not require them to declare forgiveness or take responsibility for monitoring every colleague’s behavior.

Keep the plan proportionate and properly recorded. Actual personnel details and complaint information belong in approved channels with applicable rules. Learning responses can practice the structure with invented facts: effect, action, owner, authority, check and next step if the action is not useful. A clear plan makes responsibility easier to examine and revise. It does not turn a shared conversation into a substitute for required investigation, discipline or another formal procedure.

inThisLesson: Preserve the appropriate records and routes.
lessons.keyStatement: A useful commitment is specific enough to act on and modest enough to remain within actual authority.

items.title: The commitment is only a general aspiration
items.body: Translate “communicate better” into an appropriate behavior or arrangement. For example, identify who will circulate relevant evidence before the review and who will confirm its consideration. The action should address the effect rather than merely provide a positive phrase. Check that the responsible roles can actually carry it out.

items.title: The action promises the wrong result
items.body: Considering evidence does not guarantee accepting its recommendation, and changing a meeting practice does not guarantee restored trust. State the result honestly. Do not use a repair agreement to promise employment actions or formal outcomes beyond the participants’ authority. Route those matters appropriately and preserve the separate decision process.

items.title: The check burdens the affected person
items.body: A plan that requires the employee to supervise the colleague indefinitely transfers leadership responsibility. Invite appropriate feedback without requiring continuous monitoring or emotional certification. The leader and other responsible roles should check their own actions, address remaining concerns and retain suitable formal handling.

tabs.label: Action
tabs.body: An action names the behavior or arrangement to change. Fair consideration of a contribution is different from guaranteed adoption of its recommendation. Connect the correction to the effect without bypassing the authorized decision. A clear practical action helps participants understand what will happen and avoids using a general aspiration as the entire repair plan.

tabs.label: Owner
tabs.body: An owner is the role able to perform and authorize the step. A group’s support cannot give the facilitator power over policy or personnel outcomes. Confirm dependencies and formal requirements before promising delivery. Staff and leaders carry their own responsibilities; the person affected should not become the default owner of every future improvement or monitoring task.

tabs.label: Check
tabs.body: A check asks whether the action addressed the work effect. Examine delivery, timing and usefulness separately and decide how an unresolved barrier will be handled. Do not require forgiveness as the metric. An action may need revision even when intentions were sincere, and a formal concern may continue through its own process regardless of the check.

check.question: A repair plan promises that a staff proposal will be adopted because its author experienced an exclusionary exchange. What should change?
check.correct: Preserve appropriate consideration of the evidence and responsible handling of the concern without promising a decision outcome beyond the repair plan’s authority.
wrong: Keep the promise because any repair plan can override the authorized decision process.
Remove the evidence entirely to avoid further discomfort.
Require the employee to monitor every future exchange as the only check.
check.feedbackCorrect: The plan addresses fair consideration while retaining the actual decision-maker’s responsibility.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A repair plan cannot override an authorized decision process. Removing the evidence repeats the exclusion instead of addressing consideration. Making the affected employee monitor every exchange transfers the leader’s responsibility. Preserve appropriate evidence review and formal handling without promising adoption, and assign a suitable owner and check.

items.text: The chair will circulate relevant evidence before the next review and confirm its consideration.
The discussion group guarantees adoption of a policy it cannot approve.
The employee must forgive before the action is considered successful.
The responsible role will test whether the changed participation arrangement is usable.
A shared meeting is declared to close every formal concern.
The affected employee alone must monitor colleagues indefinitely.

lessons.next: Next, review follow-through and address a recurring problem without claiming certainty from silence.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: After a project exchange, leader Nora drafts a plan promising that Emil’s proposed service change will be approved. Nora controls the meeting process but does not approve the service policy. The original effect concerned evidence being dismissed, not a promise of adoption.
options: Commit to appropriate evidence consideration and a clear handoff check, explain the decision authority, and preserve the responsible process for the concern.
Keep the approval promise so the plan feels generous.
Ask Emil to withdraw the concern before the evidence can be reviewed.
responses: This connects the action to the effect and keeps authority and formal handling clear.
A promise beyond authority is unreliable and confuses fair consideration with a guaranteed outcome.
Evidence review and support should not depend on withdrawing the concern.

lessons.transfer: Write a practice repair plan with effect, action, owner, authority boundary, check and response if the action is not useful. Remove any guaranteed outcome the owner cannot decide.

move.control: You can make an appropriate commitment specific and confirm who has authority to carry it out.
move.failure: The plan promises a formal result or relies on a feeling instead of a work change that can be checked.
move.next: Review the next suitable commitment for an identifiable owner and a realistic authority boundary.

lessons.title: Check follow-through and learn without coercion
lessons.summary: Review the action, remaining effect and appropriate next route rather than treating silence as proof of success.
lessons.objective: Distinguish completed actions from evidence that the effect improved.
objectives: Distinguish completed actions from evidence that the effect improved.
Identify a follow-up practice that pressures a person or risks retaliation.
Revise an appropriate repair plan when the action does not address the work effect.
takeaways: A completed action and a useful result are different.
Silence does not prove that a concern ended.
lessons.statement: The next check should ask what changed in the work and what still needs attention, without demanding a declaration of closure.

image.caption: A careful follow-up examines the work change rather than relying on visible comfort.

intro.heading: Learn from the action and its limits
intro.body:
A leader sends the promised information and concludes that repair is complete. The action happened, but the information still arrived after the decision. A follow-through check needs to examine both delivery and usefulness. What did the responsible role do? What effect did the action address? What remains unresolved or unknown? These questions keep the plan connected to the work instead of the leader’s wish to close the matter.

Use appropriate evidence. The revised handoff, a review record or the accessibility of a meeting arrangement may show whether a process changed. A person’s account can add relevant understanding when they choose to provide it through a suitable route. Avoid collecting more personal detail than the work question requires, storing personnel narratives in learning answers or converting individual cultural assumptions into employee labels.

Do not treat silence as proof of success. A colleague may be busy, uncertain about the follow-up, concerned about consequences or satisfied with the change. The leader cannot know which explanation is true merely because no new concern was raised. Explain an appropriate way to report whether the arrangement is useful and carry out the leader’s own check of the promised action.

Avoid pressure and retaliation. Applicable policies and law govern actual rights and responsibilities; use responsible guidance for a specific situation. Do not punish a person for using a protected route or equate honest feedback with disloyalty. At the same time, a concern does not make every ordinary work responsibility disappear. Keep decisions based on legitimate work evidence and the actual responsible process rather than invented rules from this course.

If the action did not help, revise it within authority. A late handoff might need a clear earlier point, not another apology. A recurring behavior may require a different appropriate response and formal guidance, not repeated optional discussions. The consultant can support learning and feedback; leaders and staff still carry out their responsibilities. A useful review can acknowledge limited progress, remaining uncertainty and the next accountable step without forcing an emotional ending.

lessons.keyStatement: Follow-through asks what changed, what remains and who acts next, rather than requiring proof that everyone feels resolved.

items.title: The action happened but the effect remains
items.body: Ask why the action was not useful. Timing, format or authority may have limited it. Revise the appropriate work step rather than repeating the same symbolic response. Keep formal handling and legitimate duties in place; learning from a failed action does not erase responsibility for the original concern.

items.title: No one raised a new concern
items.body: Silence leaves several possible explanations. Check the promised action directly and offer an appropriate way to share relevant feedback without repeated pressure for an emotional statement. Do not declare universal satisfaction or use the lack of a complaint as the only evidence that the process now works.

items.title: The same issue returns
items.body: Examine the supported pattern and obtain responsible guidance about the next route. Do not assume that another informal conversation is always sufficient. The actual seriousness, policy scope and facts matter. Avoid using a personal IDI label or an identity-based explanation as a substitute for examining behavior and responsibilities.

tabs.label: Delivery
tabs.body: Delivery records what actually occurred and when. Sending evidence after the decision proves a late handoff, not fair consideration before it mattered. Name the action and owner accurately instead of treating any completed email as repair. Timing and the intended work sequence are part of what needs to be checked.

tabs.label: Effect
tabs.body: Effect examines whether the contribution or arrangement changed as intended. A usable participation check may show improvement, while a missing account leaves uncertainty. Silence alone cannot establish trust or closure. Review appropriate evidence without demanding personal disclosure or penalizing the employee for not reporting the same barrier again.

tabs.label: Next step
tabs.body: A next step revises the correction within authority or uses the responsible route for a continuing issue. The leader owns follow-through on their commitment; all monitoring should not be transferred to the affected person. Explain the remaining question honestly. A practical revision can strengthen the work without promising complete emotional recovery or an unauthorized case outcome.

check.question: The promised evidence was circulated, but only after the decision. No one raises a new concern. What is the most supported conclusion?
check.correct: The action was delivered late; its intended effect is not established, and the leader should examine the timing and appropriate next step rather than claim closure from silence.
wrong: Silence proves that the timing caused no problem.
A completed email guarantees repair regardless of the decision sequence.
The employee should lose the assignment for failing to report the problem again.
check.feedbackCorrect: This distinguishes delivery, usefulness and unknown information while preserving responsible follow-through.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Silence does not show that a late handoff had no effect. A completed email cannot establish repair when the decision had already occurred. Penalizing the employee for not reporting again adds pressure instead of evidence. Examine delivery timing and intended usefulness, state the uncertainty and identify the next responsible action.

items.text: The responsible role sent the agreed information on the recorded date.
The authorized review considered the information before the decision.
No new concern means everyone forgave and trust is restored.
The chair implemented the agreed meeting arrangement.
A suitable check showed the arrangement allowed the relevant contribution.
A sincere apology guarantees the problem cannot recur.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to plan and review one appropriate work correction.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Leader Yasmin checks a repair plan after a review dispute. The promised packet was emailed after the decision, and the original contribution remains unexamined. Yasmin hears no new concern and wants to announce complete success in a team update.
scenario.prompt: Which next step is more responsible?
options: Announce complete success because no one objected again.
Check the late handoff and appropriate review route, state the remaining work question honestly, and revise the responsible action without demanding a closure statement.
Ask the affected employee to write a forgiveness statement for the update.
responses: Silence does not establish that the contribution was considered or the effect ended.
This reviews delivery and effect separately and retains accountability for the next action.
A prescribed emotional statement does not correct the handoff or provide reliable evidence.

lessons.transfer: Review an invented repair plan. List delivery evidence, effect evidence, unknowns and the next responsible action. Include a suitable route for relevant feedback without pressure.

move.control: You can check your own commitments, interpret evidence carefully and revise the action within authority.
move.failure: The leader celebrates completion while the work effect remains or pressures an employee to supply visible closure.
move.next: At the next appropriate follow-up, ask separately what was done and whether it addressed the intended work effect.

jobAid.subtitle: Prepare, carry out and review an appropriate work correction.
remember: Connect the correction to the specific effect.
A meaningful invitation has clear purpose, limits and alternatives.
Do not require forgiveness, personal disclosure or an informal conversation as an invented condition of support.
Formal workplace procedures and leader duties remain in place.
Use practice learning notes and approved channels for actual personnel information.

sections.heading: Before a conversation
items: Describe the action, reported effect and information still uncertain.
Use current responsible guidance to check suitability, policy scope, roles and actual duties.
Explain purpose, participants, limits and appropriate alternatives.
Remove hidden work penalties or a prescribed closure requirement.
Plan usable participation and an appropriate pause route.

sections.heading: During an appropriate discussion
items: Ask a neutral question about the relevant work effect.
Check understanding without announcing that every fact is settled.
Avoid forced equal blame, cultural disclosure or a required apology.
Invite a specific next responsibility within actual authority.
Pause and seek appropriate guidance when the process becomes unsuitable.

sections.heading: After the discussion
items: State the effect, action, owner, authority boundary and check.
Preserve formal routes and appropriate records.
Do not claim success from silence or require emotional certification.
Revise the action or use the responsible next route if the effect remains.

sources.title: Minnesota Office of Collaboration and Dispute Resolution — Restorative Practices
sources.note: General public information on relationships, accountability and repair. This course uses only a bounded everyday workplace application; it does not independently teach cultural traditions, facilitator methods or alternatives to required procedures.

sources.title: Minnesota Office of Collaboration and Dispute Resolution — Organizational Conflict Management
sources.note: Conflict-management resources support clear purposes, roles and suitable support. The planning exercises were developed for this course; they are not new state procedures.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Respectful Workplace Policy
sources.note: The policy defines its own scope, responsibilities, informal options and formal complaint routes. Actual agency guidance and applicable policies govern concerns; this optional course adds no blanket meeting prerequisite.

sources.title: U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission — Retaliation
sources.note: Federal guidance explains protections and legitimate work responsibilities. Actual facts, applicable law and responsible agency guidance determine a specific situation; this course does not adjudicate it.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Harassment and Discrimination Prohibited Policy 1436
sources.note: Direct authority for manager and supervisor immediate reporting and appropriate protected-class concern handling. Optional conversation or repair practices do not replace required reporting, current investigation procedure or formal decisions.
